analysis.one_liner: Lets patients bypass insurer "try a cheaper drug first" rules when the cheaper drug would harm them.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, with 36 Senate cosponsors, sat in the Senate health committee for nearly two years and died without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Insurers often use "step therapy" rules that force patients to try cheaper drugs before covering the drug their doctor prescribed, even when that could harm them. The Safe Step Act would require job-based health plans to grant an exception to those rules in specific cases, like when the required drug already failed, would cause an adverse reaction, or would keep someone from working. Plans would have to respond to exception requests within 72 hours, or within 24 hours when the delay could seriously jeopardize someone's health.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer-sponsored health coverage whose doctors prescribe a drug that the plan would only cover after "failing" on cheaper alternatives first [S2][S3]. This includes patients whose required treatment already proved ineffective, who would suffer severe or irreversible harm from a delay, who would have an adverse reaction, who cannot work or handle daily activities on the required drug, or who are already stable on the drug their doctor chose [S3]. Plans would also have to keep the patient's cost-sharing at the rates in place when they enrolled [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients with job-based insurance on prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans to grant an exception to step-therapy rules when the required drug already failed, is expected to fail with severe or irreversible consequences from delay, is likely to cause an adverse reaction, prevents the patient from working or performing daily activities, or when the patient is already stable on the prescribed drug [S2][S3].

Requires plans to run a clear, transparent exceptions process, posted on their website, that lets the prescribing doctor present clinical rationale and cannot demand paperwork beyond what is strictly necessary to decide the request [S3].

Sets hard deadlines: plans must answer an exception request within 72 hours, and within 24 hours on an expedited basis when the step-therapy protocol would seriously jeopardize the patient's life or health [S3].
Locks in the patient's cost-sharing at the rates in effect when they enrolled, so granting the exception does not come with a surprise price increase [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employer group health plans they administer (including self-insured employers) would bear higher drug spending when more patients get their originally prescribed, often costlier, drugs right away instead of being pushed through cheaper alternatives first [S3]. Step-therapy protocols exist to steer patients to lower-cost drugs, so narrowing when plans can enforce them shrinks that cost-control tool [S3]. Those costs would tend to flow back into premiums and employee contributions.

drawbacks.text: Step therapy is a cost-control tool: it pushes patients toward cheaper drugs that are often equally effective. Letting more patients skip straight to the prescribed drug would raise drug spending by plans, a cost that typically flows into premiums and employee contributions for everyone in the plan [S3].

The bill only covers group health plans under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act. People who buy their own coverage through the marketplaces, as well as Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, would get no protection from this bill [S3].

The exception criteria include a catch-all 'other circumstances as determined by the Secretary of Labor,' leaving the real scope of the mandate to future regulation rather than the statute itself [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the merits, the bill is narrowly targeted: the six exception triggers are tied to documented clinical evidence of harm, not to general preference, and the 72-hour and 24-hour deadlines give plans room to process requests. The cost is real but modest — more patients reaching costlier drugs sooner — and is the price of not forcing people to fail on drugs their doctors have already ruled out. The larger weakness is coverage: it leaves out everyone without job-based insurance. And none of this trade-off was ever tested, because the bill never advanced far enough to be debated or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with bipartisan support and sent to the Senate health committee in February 2021, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Lisa Murkowski introduced the bill on February 25, 2021 with a bipartisan group of 13 original cosponsors spanning both parties [S3].
It attracted 36 cosponsors in total: 22 of 48 Senate Democrats, 13 of 50 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 2 Senate Independents [S4].

The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress [S1][S5].
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without either chamber ever voting on it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers are better off: the step-therapy protocols the bill would have constrained remain untouched, and no federal exceptions process was created. Patients with job-based coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers

for.name: Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of 13 original cosponsors.

against.name: Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee she chaired received the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled it for a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was clearly bipartisan — 36 of 100 senators cosponsored, including 13 of 50 Republicans and 22 of 48 Democrats — but no committee or floor vote ever happened, so the actual vote split is unknown.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer group health plans
industries.note: Step-therapy protocols are a core tool insurers use to steer patients to cheaper drugs and control prescription spending. The bill would have forced them to override those protocols in six defined circumstances and answer exception requests on fixed deadlines [S3].

PBMs design and administer the utilization-management programs, including step therapy, through which plans manage drug spending. A federal exceptions process would have limited their ability to enforce those programs [S3].

Patients reaching their originally prescribed drug sooner, rather than being pushed through cheaper alternatives first, tends to mean more sales of the prescribed brand-name drug. The benefit to patients is real, but it comes partly in the form of higher drug spending by plans.
